entries.clue: Playing piano, uncle with FRCS is an accomplished pianist (7,7)

indicators.note: the letters are 'played' like notes, rearranged into a new tune

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters; 'with' just joins the pieces

annotation.surface: A surgeon uncle turns out to be a gifted pianist when he sits down at the keyboard.
annotation.walkthrough: FRCS (Fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons) looks like an abbreviation to expand, but its four letters go straight into the mix. The answer runs on into 5 across.
annotation.definitionFit: Francis Poulenc, the French composer, was also a fine concert pianist.

entries.clue: Badly dressed bum in funny clothing (6)

indicators.note: one piece sits inside another
the outside of 'funny' clothes what goes within

blocks.note: only the outer letters of 'funny' do the clothing

annotation.surface: Someone sniffing at a tramp in a ridiculous outfit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bum' reads as a vagrant, but it is the backside, RUMP. 'Funny clothing' sounds like the outfit; really it is the shell of the word 'funny'.
annotation.definitionFit: Frumpy describes dowdy, unfashionable dress.

entries.clue: Britain draping its leader in part of its coat of arms (6)

indicators.note: one piece hangs round another like cloth
the leader of 'Britain' is its first letter

blocks.clueFragment: part of its coat of arms
blocks.note: a lion supports the royal coat of arms
first letter of Britain, draped by A LION

annotation.surface: Britain as a figure half-wrapped in the heraldry of its own coat of arms.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Britain' does double duty: it is the definition, and its leader B goes inside A LION. The royal arms show a lion and a unicorn.
annotation.definitionFit: Albion is the old poetic name for Britain.

entries.clue: Run Intercity (10)

blocks.note: split the word: 'Inter' = put in the grave, and 'city' is the definition

annotation.surface: A railway timetable listing an express service.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Intercity' is a British brand of fast train, so the clue reads as a single notice; split it into 'Inter' and 'city' and the parts appear.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: split off from 'Intercity', 'city' stands for the Kent cathedral city at the end of a fast line from London.

entries.clue: Graceful woman is quiet about work-up (5)

indicators.note: one piece goes round another
in a down clue, a word going up is written backwards

blocks.note: to ply a trade is to work at it; sent up it becomes YLP

annotation.surface: A woman keeps quiet about the build-up to a job.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Work-up' looks like one word, a preparation; split it and 'up' turns PLY round.
annotation.definitionFit: A sylph is a slender, graceful girl, after the air spirits of folklore.

entries.clue: See 1
Bureaucrat in prison with drug dealer (9)

annotation.surface: An official locked up alongside a drug dealer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In prison' reads as a container instruction, but 'in' only links the definition to the wordplay, and the two pieces sit side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: A pen-pusher is a desk-bound clerk or bureaucrat.

entries.clue: Some without a happy state (4)

indicators.note: only some of the letters of the phrase are used

annotation.surface: Some people go through life without a happy state of mind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Happy state' reads as a mood; the state is American and sits across three words.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Utah is one of the fifty states of the USA, in the Mountain West.

entries.clue: Poet in residence seeing difficult birth in early James Bond premieres (1,1,6)

indicators.note: a difficult birth goes awkwardly, its letters out of order
one piece goes inside another
the premieres of words are their first letters

blocks.note: first letters of Early, James, Bond
BIRTH rearranged, placed between EJ and B

annotation.surface: A resident poet watching a film premiere with a traumatic birth scene in an early Bond movie.
annotation.walkthrough: E J Thribb is the teenage poet (always 'aged 17½') of the British satirical magazine Private Eye, who writes its mock obituary verses.
annotation.definitionFit: Thribb is Private Eye's long-standing resident poet.

entries.clue: My love, never try ear bursting, it’s a delicate body part (8,6)

indicators.note: the letters burst apart and land in a new order

blocks.note: cor! and my! are both exclamations of surprise
love = nil = O, as in tennis
nary = not one, never, as in 'nary a word'

annotation.surface: A lover warns their partner never to burst an eardrum, it being a fragile part of the body.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My love' sounds like an endearment; it is two pieces, an exclamation and the letter O. The answer runs on into 20 down.
annotation.definitionFit: The coronary arteries supply the heart, and their blockage is life-threatening.

entries.clue: Top African city describing its environment (5)

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, its first letter

blocks.note: DURBAN, the South African port, loses its first letter

annotation.surface: Praise for the best city in Africa and its surroundings.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top' reads as best; it is a verb, to behead. The definition leans on 'city': urban is the word that describes a city's environment.
annotation.definitionFit: Urban means relating to a town or city.

entries.clue: Castle at first repaired and newly restored here (9)

annotation.definition: Castle at first repaired and newly restored here

indicators.note: take the first letters of the words that follow
the letters are put back together in a new arrangement

blocks.note: first letters of Repaired, And, Newly

annotation.surface: A castle freshly repaired and renovated, in the language of a heritage notice.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition as well as the wordplay: Lancaster Castle, a prison until 2011, has since been restored and opened to visitors. It is also the Lancaster bomber that 14 across needs.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue describes Lancaster Castle, a prison until 2011 that has since been repaired and opened to visitors.

entries.clue: He was bound to catch fire? (10)

annotation.definition: He was bound to catch fire?

blocks.note: the surface reads 'he was certain to'; really he was tied down, chained to a rock
the surface reads 'ignite'; really he caught fire as a thief does, stealing it from the gods

annotation.surface: Someone certain to go up in flames.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' reads as 'certain to', and 'catch fire' as ignite. In the myth Prometheus caught (stole) fire from the gods and was bound to a rock as punishment.
annotation.definitionFit: Prometheus is the Titan who stole fire for mankind and was chained for it.

entries.clue: Architect and writer entertain on vacation (4)

indicators.note: the words are vacated, emptied of everything but their outer letters

annotation.surface: An architect and an author entertaining while away on holiday.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On vacation' sounds like holiday; here it empties both words before it. Fittingly, P C Wren was also a writer (Beau Geste).
annotation.definitionFit: Sir Christopher Wren designed St Paul's Cathedral.

entries.clue: Stuck in traffic with no toilets? A disaster (4-2-4)

indicators.note: the letters are wrecked and come out in a new order

annotation.surface: The misery of a traffic jam with nowhere to stop for the loo.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a genuine motorist's lament, so 'disaster' reads as a comment rather than an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Nose-to-tail traffic is queued bumper to bumper.

entries.clue: One looks for treasure cache, possibly among 10? (11)

indicators.note: the letters might possibly be in another order
one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: the answer to 10 across, LANCASTER, is a wartime bomber
CACHE rearranged, placed after the B of BOMBER

annotation.surface: A treasure hunter searching for a hidden hoard, perhaps near Lancaster.
annotation.walkthrough: '10' seems to point at the castle or the city; it is the Lancaster aircraft, a BOMBER.
annotation.definitionFit: A beachcomber scours the shore for anything of value.

entries.clue: Gold disc half lost, oddly no copy of recording (9)

indicators.note: only half the word is kept
no odd letters: the 1st and 3rd go, the even ones stay

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

annotation.surface: A gold disc has lost half its sales and no copies of the recording remain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gold disc' and 'half lost' look like a unit and a phrase; the split falls between them, 'disc half' and 'lost, oddly no'.
annotation.definitionFit: An audiotape is a sound recording on magnetic tape.

entries.clue: During break, workers like some bottles of wine (8)

indicators.note: one piece happens inside the span of another

blocks.note: a crew is a team of workers

annotation.surface: Staff on their break are partial to a few bottles of wine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Like some bottles' reads as the workers' taste; it is the definition, an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Many modern wine bottles have a screw-top cap instead of a cork.

entries.clue: In the morning, perhaps, in case one forgets (8)

indicators.note: the letters are perhaps in another order

annotation.surface: Advice to do something first thing, just in case you forget later.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In case' reads as a precaution; its six letters are the fodder, and the definition 'one forgets' needs 'who' understood.
annotation.definitionFit: An amnesiac is someone who suffers memory loss.
annotation.definitionNote: 'one forgets' is short for 'one who forgets'

entries.clue: Dare to break with America’s ‘special relationship’ (11)

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and reassembled

annotation.surface: A challenge to Britain to break off its much-vaunted 'special relationship' with the United States.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'special relationship' is the phrase used for the close ties between Britain and the USA; the quotation marks flag it as the definition in a looser sense.
annotation.definitionFit: The quotation marks bend 'special relationship', the political phrase for Anglo-American ties, back to its plain sense: close fellowship between friends.

entries.clue: Maroon fibre (6)

blocks.note: a verb here: to abandon someone with no way out
a single thread, as of hair or rope

annotation.walkthrough: 'Maroon' looks like a colour; here it is the verb: to strand someone is to maroon them, and a strand is also a fibre.
annotation.definitionFit: Strand means both to leave stranded and a thread.

entries.clue: See 8
Not as many start off as pitcher (4)

indicators.note: the word's starting letter is taken off

annotation.surface: Fewer people begin a baseball game as pitcher.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pitcher' suggests baseball; it is a jug.
annotation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large water jug.

entries.clue: Nursery doctor coming across outpour in bed (4-6)

indicators.note: one piece spans across another
the letters are out of order

blocks.note: Doctor Foster, who went to Gloucester in the nursery rhyme
POUR rearranged, placed after the F

annotation.surface: A children's doctor spilling something into a bed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outpour' looks like one word; split it as 'out' (the anagram signal) and 'pour'.
annotation.definitionFit: A four-poster is a bed with a post at each corner.

entries.clue: Feel sick and so forth, must be admitted to right hospital (5)

indicators.note: one piece is admitted inside the other, like a patient

annotation.surface: A patient feeling sick and worse must be admitted to hospital.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Admitted to right hospital' reads as a patient finding the correct ward; the admitting is ETC going into R and H.
annotation.definitionFit: To retch is to heave, as though about to vomit.

entries.clue: Fine and even slices of bread and vegetable (4)

indicators.note: the even-numbered letters are sliced out

blocks.note: the 2nd and 4th letters of bREAD... b-R-e-A-d

annotation.surface: A lunch of neatly cut bread and vegetables.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Even slices' sounds like neat cutting; it means the even letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Okra is a green pod vegetable, also called ladies' fingers.

entries.clue: Use one’s head swiftly when skinny kids start to abstain from food (5,4)

indicators.note: only the start of 'kids' is used

blocks.note: to fast is to go without food

annotation.surface: Quick thinking is needed when thin children start refusing to eat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swiftly' belongs to the definition: the whole of 'Use one’s head swiftly' is the phrase, and 'start' takes only the K of kids.
annotation.definitionFit: To think fast is to react quickly in the mind.

entries.clue: Open space in Casualty (5)

indicators.note: one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: A&E, Accident and Emergency, the hospital casualty department

annotation.surface: Room to breathe in a hospital's emergency ward.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Open space' reads as one phrase, a park; split it and 'Open' is the definition. A&E is the British name for a hospital emergency room, once called Casualty (also a TV drama).
annotation.definitionFit: Agape means wide open, as a mouth in surprise.

entries.clue: Had a go like crazy in swift mode of travel, etc (7,7)

indicators.note: the letters go crazy, out of order
one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: HAD A GO LIKE rearranged, placed between PAC and Y

annotation.surface: Someone tried frantically at speed while travelling.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Like crazy' is doubled up: 'like' is part of the fodder and the indicator is 'crazy'. The answer runs on into 28 across.
annotation.definitionFit: A package holiday bundles travel with accommodation and more, hence 'etc'.
